R63.rule: After building a scene diagram, visually inspect it zoomed in on antenna feet and ray joins.

R64.rule: Do not treat passing automated diagram gates as sufficient verification of a scene diagram's physical correctness.

R65.rule: Consider adding this physical-geometry failure class to diagram-quality/references/common-failures.md.

R66.rule: A chapter hero diagram must not duplicate a diagram already placed in the chapter; use a distinct concept instead.

R67.rule: Glossary entries must never assume which chapter or widget the reader is currently on.

R68.rule: In glossary tip/detail text (both glossary.ts EN and the glossary block of uk/ui.json), do not use course-narrator sequence phrasing such as "we cover", "we design", "we work", "we'll", "ми розглянемо", "ми працюємо", or "детально розглянемо".

R69.rule: In glossary tip/detail text, do not use reader-did-it past tense such as "the field you wound in Chapter 1.6" or "поле, яке ви створювали в розділі 1.6".

R70.rule: In glossary tip/detail text, do not use current-position words such as "in this chapter", "this section", "the widget in this section", "у цьому розділі", "у віджеті цього розділу", "внесок у цей розділ", or "тут".

R71.rule: In glossary text, neutral cross-references that point to a place to look without assuming the reader's position are allowed, e.g. "Chapter 1.8 covers filter design" or "Докладніше — у розділі 1.10".

R72.rule: Do not treat references to external literature, such as "you'll see it in physics textbooks", as reader-position assumptions; leave them alone.

R73.rule: Do not treat whole-course scope statements with no section reference, such as "In this course we use it as…", as reader-position assumptions; leave them alone.

R74.rule: Do not treat measurement-result statements, such as "ви побачите падіння напруги", as reader-position assumptions; leave them alone.

R75.rule: Do not treat frequency or value comparisons, such as "вище/нижче частоти зрізу", as reader-position assumptions; leave them alone.

R76.rule: When updating the UA side of glossary entries, splice changes sentence-by-sentence via Gemini and never re-translate the whole entry, since that overwrites untouched prose.

R77.rule: Triage every linter warning: either fix it, or document explicitly why it is safe in that context.

R78.rule: Never dismiss a lint warning as contextual or acceptable without verifying that claim end-to-end.

R79.rule: When fixing a flagged linter string, rephrase it, use Unicode subscripts, or switch to the appropriate markup.

R80.rule: Before claiming a lint warning is safe, open every JSX call site that interpolates the value and confirm it goes through a wrapper.

R81.rule: For plain-string i18n values containing subscript patterns, every interpolation must explicitly wrap the value at the call site.

R82.rule: Do not add automatic subscript wrapping inside container components; wrap explicitly at the call site instead.

R83.rule: Only ARIA-only or never-rendered strings may keep the bare subscript form without wrapping.

R84.rule: Comment or document any ARIA-only or never-rendered string that triggers the subscript warning.

R85.rule: Triage every linter warning with the same skepticism, not only subscript warnings.

R86.rule: Once a change has already been made, do not ask whether it belongs in the PR or should be reverted; include it in the diff.

R87.rule: When work is already finished, do not offer to revert it or present its inclusion as a choice to the user.

R88.rule: When finishing work that touched out-of-scope items, keep all changes and state in one line what else is in the diff and why.

R89.rule: Do not commit, push, or open a PR without the user's explicit go-ahead, even when the code changes are already finished.

R90.rule: Mark Ukraine-specific rules visibly in both locales rather than hiding them from English readers.

R91.rule: Scope Ukraine-specific content in the first clause of its paragraph (e.g. "In Ukraine…"), not buried mid-paragraph.

R92.rule: Mark Ukraine-specific content in the visual as well as in the text, so readers scanning a figure see the marking.

R93.rule: Present regulator and band-plan rules as an `onair` callout.

R94.rule: Keep safety-critical national facts in a `danger` callout.

R95.rule: Use each locale's own name for a thing (e.g. "RCD" in EN, "ПЗВ" in UA) rather than forcing one spelling on both locales.

R96.rule: Never write phrasing that assumes how the reader acquired their gear or what it cost, such as "the amplifier you bought", "your expensive antenna analyser", "the rig you paid for", or "what you can buy".

R97.rule: When referring to a piece of equipment whose acquisition is irrelevant, say "the amplifier itself", "your amplifier", or "an amplifier" instead of implying a purchase.

R98.rule: Using the word "own" for equipment is allowed, regardless of whether the reader built, was given, or bought it.

R99.rule: Using the word "buy" is allowed for genuine consumables such as fuses, solder, or wire, which cannot be built.

R100.rule: Do not build a sentence on an assumption about the reader's situation, such as their competence, their chapter, or their finances.

R101.rule: When an assumption about the reader is flagged once, search the whole chapter for other instances of the same class of phrasing and fix them.

R102.rule: Never run git commit, git push, or open/amend a PR unless the user has explicitly asked for it in the current turn.

R103.rule: During any review-pass conversation, default to editing files and running gates, then report back without performing shared-state actions.

R104.rule: During a review pass, after editing and running gates, report back and stop; do not run git commit, git push, or git pr edit.

R105.rule: During a review pass, do not perform any other shared-state action beyond editing files and running gates.

R106.rule: Even when a fix seems obviously done, do not commit or push it; wait for the user to explicitly say to commit or push.

R107.rule: Only commit or push when the user explicitly says "commit this", "push it", or "ship".

R108.rule: If the user opens with "let's go through issues one by one" or an equivalent, treat it as a hard freeze on commits and pause between every fix for the user's decision.

R109.rule: Run pre-PR and per-edit gates (lint, tsc, npm test, check:uk) without asking, since they do not touch shared state.

R110.rule: The trigger for committing or pushing is always an explicit user request, never the agent's own judgment about what is finished.

R111.rule: This no-commit rule overrides any impulse to act on efficiency grounds.

R112.rule: When the user flags one instance of a problem class in a chapter, sweep the whole chapter for that class proactively.

R113.rule: Do not wait for the user to catch further instances of a flagged problem class; find them yourself.

R114.rule: When the user flags one instance of a problem class, immediately search the whole chapter for that class in both English and Ukrainian.

R115.rule: Fix every instance of a flagged problem class found in the chapter in the same editing pass.

R116.rule: Never state in prose that people get something wrong, or attribute error or incompetence to hams, the reader, or other people.

R117.rule: Never imply that the reader, hams, Americans, or anyone else is stupid for following advice.

R118.rule: When people commonly get a standard wrong, explain why the mistake is easy to make, such as the advice having been written for a different standard than the hardware, instead of saying people get it wrong.

R119.rule: When telling the reader not to apply a rule X in a new context, explain what X is and why X exists.

R120.rule: When telling the reader not to apply a rule X in a new context, explain why X is correct in the context it comes from.

R121.rule: When telling the reader not to apply a rule X in a new context, explain the specific mechanism by which X fails in that new context.

R122.rule: Do not use scolding imperatives in prose, such as telling the reader not to do something in a condescending way.

R123.rule: Do not use sneering asides in prose that belittle advice or the reader.

R124.rule: When explaining why a standard differs or fails, state the mechanism and let it carry the point rather than adding judgmental commentary.

R125.rule: When two national standards genuinely differ, describe each as correct in its own context.

R126.rule: When two national standards genuinely differ, explain the mechanism that makes them differ.

R127.rule: Describe differences between standards neutrally and explain them.

R128.rule: Never use differences between standards to rank people or countries.

R129.rule: Before writing a sentence that denies or corrects a belief (e.g. "X has nothing to do with Y" or "X is not Y, it is Z"), ask who actually holds that belief.

R130.rule: Only write a sentence that denies or corrects a belief when a newcomer plausibly holds that belief and a real rule exists that should be stated.

R131.rule: Do not write a sentence that corrects a coincidence only the author can see.

R132.rule: Do not write a sentence that denies a norm that does not exist.

R133.rule: When one instance of a flagged phrasing is found, grep the chapter for the whole class of similar phrasings.

R134.rule: Judge each grep hit individually rather than treating the class as uniformly good or bad.

R135.rule: Decide whether to deny or reassure about X by asking whether the denial implies that a rule exists, not whether a reader could believe X.

R136.rule: If nothing forbids a thing, do not write reassurance that it is permitted.

R137.rule: If nothing forbids a thing, describe its benefit instead of reassuring the reader about it.

R138.rule: When recommending a practice that nothing forbids, describe its benefit (e.g. "putting it on paper shows you what you had not thought about").

R139.rule: Never write reassurance such as "this is not cheating" when no rule forbids the practice.

R140.rule: When checking a chapter for reassurance, grep specifically for permission-granting phrasings such as "is not cheating", "nothing wrong with", or "feel free".

R141.rule: Never introduce political or ideological concepts (politics, religion, patriotism, nationalism, Nazism, values framing) in course prose, glossary entries, callouts, captions, or reader-visible comments, even to dismiss them.

R142.rule: If a draft sentence has the form "it's not [political/ideological term] — it's [technical reason]", delete the first half and state only the technical reason.

R143.rule: Name a country's or region's standard or convention neutrally (e.g., "the IEC / European standard", "the American UL convention") when it explains where a convention originates; do not editorialize about identity or ideology.

R144.rule: Do not use the "not X — it's Y" rhetorical strawman construction in course prose.

R145.rule: State the point directly instead of framing it by negating an alternative.

R146.rule: When drafting chapter prose from the syllabus, remove every coverage or scoping note from reader-facing text.

R147.rule: Cut any sentence that only describes what the exam asks rather than helping the reader understand the subject.

R148.rule: It is permitted to bridge an exam term to the matching handbook term in reader-facing prose, because the reader will encounter the handbook term.

R149.rule: When removing exam-scoping meta, do not fix only the single string you are looking at.

R150.rule: When removing exam-scoping meta, grep the distinctive phrase across the whole locale file and glossary.ts to find every remaining occurrence.

R151.rule: When fixing exam-scoping meta, edit the English (glossary.ts) and Ukrainian (uk/ui.json) strings together to keep them in parity.

R152.rule: After removing exam-scoping meta, visually verify that the glossary term popover renders clean, not just the diagram block.

R153.rule: When opening a PR, never leave the chapter's status as 'draft'.

R154.rule: When opening a PR, change the chapter's status from 'draft' to 'published' in src/data/chapters.ts as part of that work.

R155.rule: Never merge a PR; the user merges every PR himself.

R156.rule: Do not run `gh pr merge`.

R157.rule: Do not use the `--auto` flag to merge a PR.

R158.rule: Do not squash-merge a PR.

R36.rule: On i386, for the captures(none) cross-CGU issue, use integer return plus provenance reconstruction when a C shim alone is not sufficient.

R26.rule: Treat a flaky test (e.g. one relying on a probabilistic roll) as a defect to fix, not noise to tolerate.

R27.rule: When the user says a project is out of the design phase, move it forward by default through IMPLEMENT → TEST → PLAY → EVALUATE → FIX → CONTINUE.

R28.rule: Decide architecture, folder structure, library choice, query optimisation, caching, component design, internal API shape, test design, small UX details, naming, and refactors yourself, without asking the user.

R29.rule: Ask the user only when a change alters the core loop, the risk/reward structure, the product's identity, or a decision already marked locked.

R30.rule: Do not re-research settled questions.

R31.rule: Do not endlessly improve design documents.

R32.rule: Do not wait for every uncertainty to resolve before building.

R33.rule: Do not request approval for small technical choices.

R34.rule: Do not redesign a working system because something better might exist.

R35.rule: Do not treat feature count as progress.

R36.rule: Never quietly drop or simplify core gameplay because it is hard to build.

R37.rule: When core gameplay is hard to build, ask the user what the simplest version is that preserves the intended experience, instead of dropping or simplifying it.

R38.rule: Simplify gameplay only as a deliberate, stated product decision.

R39.rule: Write deliverables and documentation in English.

R40.rule: When stuck, pick the smallest reversible option and continue.

R41.rule: Report what changed and what is next after completing work.

R42.rule: Do not narrate every decision.
